passage:
Subject: a favour, and an honest one
Dear Noor,
You know I've been leading the new library project in Srinagar for a month now. People have started laughing at my jokes a little too hard, and that scares me. So here's the favour: stay the friend who tells me when I'm wrong. You did it in college about my terrible debate speech, and you were right.
A few things I'm trying. Every Friday I ask the team one question: what did my decisions this week cost you? Last week Imran said the new hours meant he missed his daughter's bedtime. We changed them. When the district officer praised the reading corner, I made sure he knew Shazia built it.
If I start sounding pleased with myself, say so. Please.
With love, and a thick skin,
Hafsa

qa.q: What question does Hafsa ask the team every Friday?
qa.a: Hafsa asks: what did my decisions this week cost you?

qa.q: Why does Hafsa feel scared when people laugh at the jokes too hard?
qa.a: Hafsa worries it means people are starting to please the leader instead of being honest, the first step toward self-importance.

qa.q: What did Hafsa change after Imran spoke up, and what does that choice show?
qa.a: Hafsa changed the new hours after Imran said he missed his daughter's bedtime, showing the Friday question leads to real action.

qa.q: How might Shazia feel when the district officer learns who built the reading corner?
qa.a: Shazia would likely feel seen and valued, since Hafsa passed the credit on instead of keeping the praise.

grounding: A young project leader's email asks a friend for honest pushback and describes asking what decisions cost the team and sharing credit.

passage: Okay, Anirban, the honest version. When I became head guide for the Yuksom treks at twenty-four, the porters and younger guides started calling me Dolma-la, and I liked it more than I should have. Then one morning Pemba, my friend since school, said, 'You didn't ask anyone before changing the camp site.' It stung. He was right. So I made rules for myself. Before a big decision, I ask the porters what it costs them: heavier loads, extra walking. I keep Pemba and two others who argue with me close, and I thank them when they do. When a group writes a nice review, I read it out at dinner with every name in it. It's not saintliness. I watched the guide before me slowly stop hearing people, and I don't want that drift.

qa.q: What did Pemba say one morning?
qa.a: Pemba said, 'You didn't ask anyone before changing the camp site.'

qa.q: How did Dolma feel about Pemba's remark?
qa.a: It stung, but Dolma felt Pemba was right, after admitting to liking the title Dolma-la more than was wise.

qa.q: Which of Dolma's habits turned that sting into lasting change?
qa.a: Asking porters what a decision costs them, keeping friends who argue close, and reading reviews aloud with every name keep Dolma listening instead of drifting.

qa.q: How might the porters see Dolma asking them before a big decision?
qa.a: The porters are likely to feel respected and freer to speak honestly, since their loads and extra walking now count 🙂

grounding: A young head guide tells how they invite disagreement, weigh costs to porters and share credit to avoid drifting into self-importance.

passage:
I've worked beside Shankar at the bus depot workshop for three years, so when he was made shift in-charge at twenty-five, I waited to see what would happen. Some people change overnight. Shankar didn't, or not that I could see. The first week he pinned a sheet on the notice board: 'What's one thing I got wrong this week? Drop it in the box, no names.' I thought it was for show. But on Monday he read two of them out and changed the tea-break roster because of one. When the depot manager praised the quick repair of bus 42, Shankar pointed at old Yellappa and me. He still eats lunch on the same bench. I can't tell you what goes on in his head; maybe he's scared of becoming like the last in-charge. From outside, it just looks like he keeps asking.
— Lokesh

qa.q: What did Shankar's sheet on the notice board ask?
qa.a: It asked, 'What's one thing I got wrong this week?'

qa.q: What does Lokesh think might be going on in Shankar's head?
qa.a: Lokesh guesses Shankar might be scared of becoming like the last in-charge, while admitting not knowing for sure.

qa.q: Which choice convinced Lokesh the sheet was not just for show?
qa.a: On Monday Shankar read two of the notes out and changed the tea-break roster because of one.

qa.q: How might Yellappa feel when Shankar points to Yellappa after the manager's praise?
qa.a: Yellappa would likely feel respected and noticed, since the new in-charge shared the credit for repairing bus 42.

grounding: A colleague describes a new shift in-charge who invites anonymous criticism, acts on it and shares credit, without claiming to know his mind.

passage:
Monday, week one. Hrithik, twenty-five, was made site lead of a rooftop solar crew. At the first tea break he said, "I'm new at this. Tell me when I get it wrong," and handed out a slip of paper to each worker. Most came back blank.

Thursday, week three. The client wanted the job done by Sunday. Hrithik was ready to order Sunday work, then stopped and asked, "What does this cost you?" Pankaj, the oldest fitter, said flatly, "My son's school function." Two others had similar reasons. Hrithik moved two panels' work to Friday evening instead and asked Pankaj to keep telling him when he disagreed.

Saturday, week six. The company owner praised the fast job. Hrithik read out the names of every fitter, Pankaj first. That week, eight slips came back with writing on them.

qa.q: What did Hrithik hand out at the first tea break?
qa.a: He handed out a slip of paper to each worker.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik ask Pankaj to keep telling him when he disagreed?
qa.a: He seemed wary of drifting into giving orders without listening, and wanted to stay aware of what his decisions cost the crew.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how the crew responded to Hrithik?
qa.a: After he changed the Sunday plan and gave credit by name, the crew began to trust him, and eight slips came back with writing on them.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Hrithik after the Sunday decision?
qa.a: Pankaj might see a young lead who actually listens, which makes Pankaj more willing to speak honestly in the future.

grounding: A young site lead invites honest feedback, asks what decisions cost his crew, keeps a disagreeing voice close and shares credit.

passage: Sit, Anand. They made you team lead today, so let an old man tell you what I did when I got my first crew at the printing press. I was twenty-five, younger than most of them. Old Joseph, who ran the big machine, told me on my first day, "Everyone turns into a small king. Watch yourself." So I did three things. Every Friday I asked each man, "What did my decisions cost you this week?" Once it was a missed train, once a lost weekend. I fixed what I could. I kept Joseph close, even though he argued with me in front of everyone, and I thanked him for it. And when the owner praised a rush job, I said the names of the men who stayed up. Tarun Sir, they called me. I made sure it never went to my head.

qa.q: What did Old Joseph warn Tarun about on the first day?
qa.a: He said everyone turns into a small king and told him to watch himself.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep Joseph close even though Joseph argued with him?
qa.a: He wanted someone honest enough to disagree, because he was afraid of drifting into self-importance as Joseph had warned.

qa.q: Which of Tarun's habits might help Anand most in his new role, and why?
qa.a: Asking each week what Anand's decisions cost the team keeps Anand curious about the people below, so problems like a missed train get fixed.

qa.q: How might the crew have seen a young boss who named them in front of the owner?
qa.a: They would likely feel valued and trust him more, since he shared credit instead of taking it.

grounding: An elder remembers how, as a young leader, he asked for honest feedback, kept a disagreeing voice close and shared credit to avoid self-importance.

passage: The monsoon had flooded half the villages the NGO served, and Hafsa, twenty-five, had just been made field lead. The relief plan had to be finalised by noon. She could have written it alone; the director trusted her. Instead she called the field workers together in the leaky office. "Tell me what's wrong with my plan. Honestly." Pankaj, who'd been there longer than her, frowned. "You've sent the trucks to the main road. The hamlets past the river are cut off. We'd have to carry supplies on foot." Hafsa felt a flash of irritation, then asked, "What would that cost your team?" "Four extra hours. But the hamlets need it most." She changed the plan. When the director praised it that evening, Hafsa said, "Pankaj caught the gap. The credit's his."

qa.q: How many extra hours would carrying supplies on foot take?
qa.a: Four extra hours.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Pankaj criticised the plan?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a flash of irritation but stayed curious, choosing to listen rather than defend her plan.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's habits guards against self-importance, and why?
qa.a: She invited honest criticism, asked what her decision cost the team and shared credit, which kept her attentive to others.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Hafsa credited him to the director?
qa.a: Pankaj likely felt respected and valued, more willing to speak up again.

grounding: A young leader invites honest feedback, asks what her decision costs those below her and shares credit, staying curious about others under time pressure.

passage: Tarun, twenty-six, had just become the youngest team lead at his Bengaluru start-up. On his first day, he did something unusual: he took his old friend Kiran for chai and said, "You're the one person who'll tell me when I'm being an idiot. Please keep doing it." Kiran laughed. "Easy." Three weeks later, Tarun pushed a deadline that meant the team would work through a weekend. Kiran caught him at the lift. "You're being an idiot. Half the team has family events." Tarun's pride flared. Then he remembered his own request. He asked the team directly what the weekend would cost them. It was a lot. He moved the deadline by four days and told the client himself. At the next review he named two juniors whose work had saved the project. Kiran raised his cup across the room.

qa.q: By how many days did Tarun move the deadline?
qa.a: He moved the deadline by four days.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Kiran called him an idiot at the lift?
qa.a: Tarun felt a flare of wounded pride, then remembered his request and chose to listen.

qa.q: Why was asking Kiran to keep telling him the truth a wise move?
qa.a: Keeping a friend who will disagree helps Tarun notice when power starts making him careless about others.

qa.q: How might the juniors feel when Tarun named them at the review?
qa.a: The juniors likely felt proud and valued, seeing their lead share credit publicly.

grounding: A young team lead keeps a friend who will disagree, asks what his deadline costs the team, and shares credit, limiting the drift toward self-importance.

passage:
"Trisha, got a minute before service?"
"Sure, chef." Trisha wiped her hands.
"You've been on this line three years. I got head chef two weeks ago. What am I doing badly?"
Trisha blinked. "Honestly?"
"That's the only way I want it."
"You changed the prep schedule without asking. Now the morning crew comes in an hour earlier and nobody told them why."
Rehana winced. "What did that cost them?"
"Buses. Kids' school drop. Suresh has been coming in late and getting shouted at."
"By me."
"By you."
Rehana was quiet. "Okay. I'll talk to the crew today and we'll fix the schedule together. And Trisha, tell me again when I mess up."
"You really want that?"
"I really need that." Rehana smiled. "Also, your sauce idea from Tuesday? I'm putting your name on the menu."

qa.q: How long has Trisha been on the line?
qa.a: Trisha has been on this line three years.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she heard about Suresh?
qa.a: Rehana felt uncomfortable and regretful, realising her schedule change had hurt the crew.

qa.q: Which of Rehana's actions show humility safeguards?
qa.a: She asked for honest feedback, asked what her decision cost the crew, planned to fix it together, and put Trisha's name on the menu.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel about being asked for honesty?
qa.a: Trisha was surprised at first but likely felt trusted and respected by the new head chef.

grounding: A young head chef invites honest feedback, asks what her decision costs her staff, and shares credit to guard against self-importance.

passage:
When I was made project lead last year, at twenty-five, my first fear was turning into the boss I'd hated. I'm Divyansh, and I did three things on purpose.
First, I kept Lalit close. He's my oldest friend at the firm and loves to argue. When I proposed weekend work, he said, "Ask the juniors what it costs them first." I did. Two of them had exams. We moved it.
Second, every Friday I asked the team one question: "What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"
Third, when the client praised the report, I read out the names of the two juniors who'd built it.
It's not perfect. But I still hear things I don't want to hear, and that feels right.

qa.q: What question did Divyansh ask the team every Friday?
qa.a: "What's one thing I did this week that didn't help?"

qa.q: What was Divyansh afraid of when made project lead?
qa.a: Divyansh was afraid of becoming the kind of boss once hated, and so felt the need to guard against it.

qa.q: Which of Divyansh's habits seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Lalit close is useful, because an honest friend who disagrees catches mistakes like the weekend work before they hurt people.

qa.q: How might the two juniors feel when their names are read out to the client?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and valued, knowing the lead shared the credit.

grounding: Shows a young leader inviting honest feedback, keeping a friend who disagrees, asking what decisions cost juniors and sharing credit.

passage:
Mentor's note, three months into Gautam's first role as shift supervisor.
Gautam is twenty-four and runs a team of nine at the call centre. I've watched him closely. He does something unusual: at the end of each shift, he asks one agent, "What made today harder?" Leela told him that the new break schedule meant she missed her bus. He changed it the next day.
He also keeps a friend from his training batch, who is now a peer, as his "disagree person." They have lunch every week.
When the team hit its target, he sent the regional manager a list of names, not his own.
I've advised him to keep these habits when the pressure rises.

qa.q: How many people are in Gautam's team?
qa.a: He runs a team of nine.

qa.q: What does Gautam's question "What made today harder?" suggest about how he feels toward his team?
qa.a: It suggests he feels curious and caring about his team, wanting to see the costs of his decisions.

qa.q: What habit should Gautam keep as the pressure rises?
qa.a: He should keep asking agents what made the day harder, since it shows the costs of his decisions early.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when the break schedule changes the next day?
qa.a: Leela would likely feel heard and grateful that her problem was fixed so quickly.

grounding: Shows a young leader asking what his decisions cost people below him, keeping a friend who disagrees and sharing credit.

passage:
Wednesday
Today my first month as warehouse lead ended. I'm Manoj, and I want to write this down before I forget why I started.
Pankaj, who has been here longer than me, told me in the canteen that my new loading order makes the old workers walk twice as far. My first reaction was irritation. I'm the lead now. Then I remembered Pankaj was the one who taught me the ropes.
So I walked the route myself this afternoon. He was right. Tomorrow I'll change it and tell everyone Pankaj spotted it.
Note to self: every week, ask one person what my decisions cost them. Keep Pankaj close, even when he annoys me.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say about the new loading order?
qa.a: He said it makes the old workers walk twice as far.

qa.q: What was Manoj's first reaction to Pankaj, and what does it show?
qa.a: Manoj first felt irritated, which shows the pull of feeling important as the new lead.

qa.q: Which choice helps Manoj stay a good lead, and why?
qa.a: Walking the route to check Pankaj's point and then crediting Pankaj keeps Manoj curious about others and shares credit.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel when Manoj tells everyone Pankaj spotted it?
qa.a: Pankaj would likely feel respected and valued for speaking up.

grounding: Shows a young leader checking a decision's cost to workers, keeping an honest colleague close and sharing the credit.

passage: When Deepak was elected head of the farmers' cooperative in Sangola at twenty-five, the oldest member, Madhav Kaka, warned him: 'The chair changes people. Watch yourself.' Deepak took it seriously. He kept eating lunch at the same tea stall with the farmers, not in the new office. He put a box outside the office door for anonymous complaints and read every slip on Sunday. Before deciding the new water-sharing schedule, he walked the fields at the tail end of the canal, asking the smallest farmers what the change would cost them. When the plan worked, he stood back at the meeting and said, 'Madhav Kaka and the tail-end farmers designed this.' Madhav Kaka, who had argued with him at every meeting, grinned. 'Still the same boy. Good.'

qa.q: Where did Deepak keep eating lunch?
qa.a: At the same tea stall with the farmers.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt hearing Madhav Kaka's warning?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt respect mixed with caution, taking the warning seriously enough to build habits against it.

qa.q: Which habits kept Deepak humble?
qa.a: Eating with the farmers, reading anonymous complaints, asking the smallest farmers about costs and sharing credit publicly.

qa.q: How does Madhav Kaka see Deepak after the meeting?
qa.a: Madhav Kaka is pleased and proud, seeing that the chair hasn't changed Deepak.

grounding: A young cooperative head in a village guards against power's drift by staying close, inviting critics and sharing credit.

passage: When Siddiq became the youngest manager at the Warsaw logistics office, he wrote three rules on a sticky note inside his desk drawer: Ask who pays. Keep a critic. Give the credit away. His critic was Marek, a warehouse supervisor twenty years older who had openly doubted he could do the job. Siddiq invited him to every planning meeting. 'Tell me when I'm wrong,' he said. Marek did, often. When Siddiq wanted to move the night shift to cut costs, Marek said the older drivers couldn't sleep in the day. Siddiq went to the warehouse at 3 am and asked the drivers himself. He changed the plan. At the quarterly meeting, when the new routes saved money, he put Marek's name on the first slide. Marek grunted. 'You're less annoying than I expected.'

qa.q: What three rules did Siddiq write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Ask who pays. Keep a critic. Give the credit away.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he invited his doubter to every meeting?
qa.a: Siddiq felt humble and curious, wanting honest criticism to guard against his own blind spots.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do before changing the night shift?
qa.a: He went to the warehouse at 3 am, asked the drivers himself, and then changed the plan.

qa.q: How does Marek's view of Siddiq change?
qa.a: Marek goes from openly doubting Siddiq to grudging respect, saying he's less annoying than expected.

grounding: A young manager abroad keeps a critic close, asks what decisions cost those below him and shares credit.

passage: Omkar was twenty-six and the youngest head chef the hotel kitchen had ever had. Every Friday after the dinner rush, he pulled up an upturned crate and asked the same question: "What did I get wrong this week?" The first month, nobody answered. Then Jagdish, the oldest cook, said, "The new 6 am prep shift. You didn't ask who takes the first bus." Three of the dishwashers came from villages an hour away. Omkar went quiet, then moved prep to seven. When a food critic praised the new mango kulfi, Omkar pointed at the pastry section. "Ask Lata. It's her recipe." Some nights he rang an old friend from catering college who never let him win an argument. "Still humble, chef?" "Trying," Omkar said.

qa.q: What time did Omkar move the prep shift to?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: Why did Omkar go quiet after Jagdish spoke?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a little ashamed to realise his 6 am shift had cost the dishwashers who took the first bus, and he wanted to fix it.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's habits guard against self-importance?
qa.a: Asking every Friday what he got wrong, crediting Lata for the kulfi, and keeping a friend who argues with him all keep him curious about others.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel after the prep shift moved?
qa.a: Jagdish would likely feel respected and trusted, seeing that honest feedback to the young chef actually changed things.

grounding: A young head chef invites honest feedback, asks what his decisions cost his staff, shares credit and keeps a friend who disagrees.
